--- title: "Tutorial" engine: julia execute: freeze: auto --- *First steps are always small* The author tried to make this as user-friendly as possible. It is hoped, but not guranteed, that the user will not require to look into the source code! Here's a walkthrough of to perform a simulation using this library. ## Mesh definition and precomputations The library was built up to provide differentiability for a specific use-case: Sensitivity analyses of Avalanches. As such, OpenFoam offers support for generating finite area meshes or surface-discretizations. Thus, the library requires the mesh to be in OpenFoam's format. For general support with any 3D model, please generate the mesh using OpenFoam's [avalanche](https://develop.openfoam.com/Community/avalanche) module. Once the files are generated, look into `constant\polyMesh` and `constant\faMesh` for the files `points`, `faces` and `faceLabels` files. Once that's done, here's how you should proceed. ```julia import FASolverAvalanche as FAS # Model Parameters const alpha = 0.5 # Pressure Model const zeta = 1.25 # Velocity Model const rho = 1500.0 # Density # Define the requirements mesh = FAS.Mesh( location_points = "./data/points", location_faces = "./data/faces", location_faceLabels = "./data/faceLabels", threads= true, stats = true, FLOAT_TYPE = Float32 ) FAS.init(mesh) # Initialize the library Cells, points, faces = FAS.preprocess(mesh) # Parse the library and precompute geometry ``` The library defines a struct `Mesh` for a combined user-interface for parsing and preprocessing the geometry. This approach is useful as it allows the user to perform computations in user-defined datatypes. The function `init` initializes the library and initializes some global variables. The `preprocess` function performs the parsing and precomputations on the geometry and stores it in the `Cell` struct. The structure acts as a cache containing geometrical information to be used at runtime and also allocates some memory to store variables at runtime. This reduces runtime-allocations and makes the solver more efficient. Non-orthogonal cells can be using the `vizNonOrthogonal` function as: ```julia FAS.vizNonOrthogonal(Cells, points, faces) ```
## Defining Initial and boundary conditions The free surface flow equations of the Savage Hutter model typically don't require boundary conditions. To handle the boundary, the solver uses a zero-gradient (Neumann) schemes. User-defined boundary conditions are not yet supported. Boundary conditions can help simulate inflow and outflow. Zero-gradient being the easiest to realize in code was chosen to represent the boundary. The solver is therefore currently limited to flows without external inflow and outflow. Initial conditions are given using a polygonal release area. Spherical release areas are not directly supported. But, remeber, a polygonal with infinite vertices approaches a circle :) Here's how initial conditions are defined: ```julia FAS.meshBounds(cells) FAS.meshBounds(vertices) polygon = FAS.findRegularPolygon([5.0, 10.0, -3.0,3.0], npoints=6) cells_inside = FAS.cellsInsideBoundingPolygon(polygon, Cells) FAS.initializeGeometry(cells_inside, Cells, rho, h0 = 0.5, vel0 = [0.0,0.0,0.0] ) ``` The `meshBounds` function gives the bounding region of the surface, i.e., the limits of **x** and **y** coodinates when the surfaces is projected onto the **xy** plane. This information can be used to assign different initial conditions in different parts of the mesh. The function `findRegularPolygon` finds a regular polygon inside a given rectangular region defined using ``[x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max]``. The supporting function `cellsInsideBoundingPolygon` finds all cells which lie inside the polygon. This is then passed to the `initializeGeometry` function which assigns the given value for thickness **h** and velocity vector **u** (in global coordinates) as specified. For a composure of initial conditions, it is possible to have multiple bounding polygons with different intial conditons like: ```julia polygon1 = FAS.findRegularPolygon() polygon2 = FAS.findRegularPolygon() cells_inside1 = FAS.cellsInsideBoundingPolygon(polygon1, Cells) cells_inside2 = FAS.cellsInsideBoundingPolygon(polygon2, Cells) ``` For even more complex initial conditions, it is also possible to iterate over the `Cells` vector directly. ```julia for i in eachindex(Cells) Cells[i].h = h_initial[i] # h_initial is defined before hand Cells[i].vel = vel_initial[i] # vel_initial is defined before hand end ``` If the initial polygons intersect, the maximum of all the values will be chosen as the value at the cell. ```julia # First Polygon polygon1 = FAS.findRegularPolygon([5.0, 10.0, -3.0,3.0], npoints=6) cells_inside = FAS.cellsInsideBoundingPolygon(polygon1, Cells) FAS.initializeGeometry(cells_inside, Cells, rho, h0 = 0.5, vel0 = [0.0,0.0,0.0] ) # Second Polygon polygon2 = FAS.findRegularPolygon([15.0,10.0,-5.0,15.0], npoints=5) cells_inside = FAS.cellsInsideBoundingPolygon(polygon2, Cells) FAS.initializeGeometry(cells_inside, Cells, rho, h0 = 0.3, vel0 = [0.0,0.0,1e-2]) # Different boundary conditions ``` > **_NOTE:_** Choose the initial polygon properly. If the polygon is too big, the solver might require some stabilization by appropriate choice of parameters. This however is not straightforward and might take several iterations to figure. ## Setting up the solver and final solution process Once the initial conditions are set up, setting up the solver is simple. Create a structure `Solution` and pass it to the `Solver` function to create a `solver` object. The `solver` object contains the precomputed geometry and user choices for controlling the solution (relaxation factors, linear solvers, preconditioners, tolerances, etc.) Here's an example, ```julia solution = FAS.Solution( Cells = Cells, alpha = alpha, zeta = zeta, rho = rho, MAX_ITERS=50, MIN_ITERS = 6, h_MAX_RESIDUAL = 1e-2, u_MAX_RESIDUAL = 1e-2, alpha_h = 0.5, alpha_u = 0.5 ) ``` Once this is done, creating a solver is straightforward. ```julia solver = FAS.Solver(solution) ``` Finally, it's time for solution. The `solve` function takes in the `solver` and starts the iteration process. Here's how the solve function should be used: ```julia time_steps, sol = FAS.solve(solver, (0.0,15.0), saveat=0.2) ``` The second argument to the `solve` function is the tspan denoting the time the flow should be simulated. The function uses adaptive timestepping based on the Courant number to solve the equations. To have the solution saved at uniform timesteps, use the `saveat` argument denoting the uniform timestep, the solution needs to be saved at. The optional parameter `Cₘ` defines the maximum Courant number and can be used to control step-sizes for timestepping. ## Post-processing The library offers limited visualization support by itself. It uses the `Makie` framework along with `GLMakie` to have a 3D visualization of the surface. Here's how: ```julia import GLMakie as Mke mesh = FAS.createVizMesh(points, faces) h = [sol[end][5*idx-4] for idx in eachindex(Cells)] FAS.viz(mesh, showsegments=true, showfacets=true, color=h) ``` An example visualizing the solution at the final timestep. An issue with this is that `GLMakie` uses a default colorscheme for coloring the faces. This might not give good results visually. It is up to the user to put in the extra effort of defining a colorscheme themselves. Animations can be made using a series of `PNG` files saved as, ```julia for i in eachindex(sol) h = [sol[i][5*idx-4] for idx in eachindex(Cells)] scene = FAS.viz(mesh, showsegments=true, showfacets=true, color=h) Mke.save("./solution/time_"*String(Symbol(i))*".png", scene) end ``` A much better alternative is to export the solution to ParaView. The library offers a `writeToVTK` function to write the solution in terms of `VTK` files. ```julia FAS.writeToVTK("./solution/", sol, points, faces) ``` > **_NOTE:_** To avoid overwritting issues, the `writeToVTK` function deletes the contents of the given directory and then saves the new VTK files. It is recommended to create an empty directory for saving the solution to avoid losing other files. And that's it. You solved the free surface flow equations and simulated avalanches on your geometry! ### WILL ADD DOCUMENTATION FOR DIFFERENTIABILITY LATER
